recipe.history:
Whiskey is one of humanity's oldest and most globally distributed distilled spirits, with roots stretching back to medieval monastic Ireland and Scotland, where monks distilled fermented grain mash into what they called uisce beatha — the water of life. The earliest documented reference to Scotch whisky dates to 1494, when the Exchequer Rolls of Scotland recorded a friar receiving malt to produce aqua vitae. Irish whiskey followed a parallel development, and the two traditions diverged in technique over the centuries — Scotch leaning toward malted barley and pot-still double distillation, Irish embracing triple distillation for a smoother profile. American whiskey, particularly bourbon, emerged as settlers pushed westward into Kentucky and Tennessee in the late eighteenth century, finding that the local limestone-filtered water, the abundance of corn, and the climate — hot summers and cold winters cycling spirit through charred oak barrels — produced something categorically different: sweeter, fuller, and more vanilla-forward than its Old World ancestors. Bacon, for its part, has ancient provenance across nearly every culture that kept pigs, with cured and smoked pork belly found in Chinese culinary records as far back as 1500 BCE and Roman lardum serving as the cured pork fat that powered legions across the empire.

The marriage of whiskey and bacon in American cooking is a romance born from the same culture of smoke, char, and preservation that defines the American barbecue tradition. Bourbon in particular began appearing in glazes and brines as early as the nineteenth century in Kentucky and Tennessee, where cooks discovered that the spirit's sugars caramelized magnificently over heat, creating a lacquer of deep, complex sweetness on smoked and grilled meats. By the mid-twentieth century, bacon-wrapped everything was a staple of American cookout culture, and the idea of adding whiskey to the bacon glaze — a double layering of smoky, sweet, savory intensity — was an inevitable evolution. In the burger world, whiskey glazed bacon arrived as a topping sometime in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when gastropubs and premium burger joints began experimenting with deconstructing and rebuilding the classic American cheeseburger with craft ingredients. The combination played on every register the palate has: sweet from the whiskey reduction, salty from the bacon, smoky from the char, fatty and rich from the pork.

I first made a whiskey bacon glaze on a dare from my brother-in-law, who bet me that I couldn't make bacon taste better than it already did. I accepted without hesitation. I rendered thick-cut strips low and slow until the fat turned translucent and the edges crisped, then deglazed the pan with a reckless pour of rye whiskey — it went up in a small, beautiful flame that singed my eyebrows slightly and filled the kitchen with a smell I can only describe as ambition. I added brown sugar, a hit of apple cider vinegar, some Worcestershire, and watched the whole thing reduce into a shining, sticky, mahogany glaze that clung to each strip like lacquer on fine furniture. When I placed those strips on the burger and my brother-in-law took his first bite, he was quiet for a long time. Then he said, simply, 'okay.' That is the highest praise he has ever given anyone for anything, and I hold it close.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not carelessness — it is precision. The window between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit is where the Maillard reaction on the exterior has built a proper seared crust while the interior retains the pink, warm, yielding texture that makes each bite taste like the beef was cooked with respect. The whiskey bacon glaze demands this temperature — its sweetness and richness require the juiciness of a medium-rare patty to balance it, a sort of richness counterbalanced by the moisture still alive in the meat. A well-done patty would make the whole thing cloying and dry. Medium rare keeps the contrast intact, keeps the beef the star even as the bacon and whiskey perform their duet above it.
instructions: 1. Make the buns: In a large bowl, whisk together warm milk, sugar, and yeast. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add softened butter and egg; mix to combine. Add bread flour and salt. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 4 portions, shape into smooth balls, flatten slightly, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Let rise 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

3. Make the whiskey glaze: Combine whiskey, brown sugar, apple cider vinegar, Worcestershire, Dijon, smoked paprika, and cayenne in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring to dissolve sugar. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the glaze coats the back of a spoon and has reduced by roughly half. Remove from heat.

4. Cook the bacon: Lay bacon strips in a cold cast-iron skillet. Set heat to medium-low. Cook slowly, 6–8 minutes per side, until the fat is rendered and the strips are nearly crisp but still have some chew. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. Drain most of the fat from the skillet, leaving a thin coating.

5. Glaze the bacon: Brush the whiskey glaze generously over both sides of the cooked bacon strips using a pastry brush. Return strips to the skillet over medium-low heat for 60–90 seconds per side until the glaze caramelizes and turns glossy. Watch carefully to avoid burning. Transfer to a rack set over a baking sheet and let cool slightly — the glaze will firm up as it sits.
6. Make the burger sauce: Whisk together mayonnaise, ketchup, yellow mustard, pickle brine, and onion powder. Taste and adjust. Refrigerate until ready to use.

7. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a dimple in the center. Season generously with kosher salt and pepper on both sides just before cooking.

8. Cook the patties: Return the skillet (with its thin coating of bacon fat) to high heat. Once very hot, add patties. Sear without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Add a slice of sharp cheddar to each patty. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast the buns cut-side down in the skillet for 60–90 seconds until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread burger sauce on both bun halves. Place the cheddar-topped patty on the bottom bun. Layer 2 strips of whiskey-glazed bacon over the patty. Add tomato slices, iceberg lettuce, raw onion slices, and pickle chips. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately.
